JUDGMENT
ON A MOTION OF PETITIONER D. J. TO INSTITUTE A PROTECTIVE SUPERVISION FOR A
PERSON OF FULL AGE

and

ON
A MOTION OF CURATOR PUBLIC DU QUÉBEC TO REVOKE A MANDATE IN CASE OF
INCAPACITY AND TO INS­­­­­­­­­TITUTE PROTECTIVE SUPERVISION

(Art.
256, et seq. and 2177 C.C.Q. and 877 et seq.
C.C.P.)

______________________________________________________________________

[
1
]

The Court is seized with two similar Motions,
one filed on November 24, 2011 by Mr. D. J. (“
J.
”), the husband of the
Respondent, Mrs. De. P. (“
De.
”) (the “
J. Motion
”) and a second
one filed on December 27, 2013 by the Curateur Public du Québec (the “
Curator
”)
(the “
Curator Motion
”).

[
2
]

In his Motion, J. is seeking the following
conclusions:

“
DECLARE
De. P. permanently unfit to take care of her person and to administer
her property;

TO DECLARE
the institution of a protective supervision of curatorship of the
person and property of De. P.;

TO APPOINT
, J. curator of the person and property of De. P.;

WAIVER
of holding a family council and psychosocial evaluation;

ORDER
the respondent to return to her home with the petitioner;

Subsequently,
ORDER
any
other decision appropriate to the file;

TO ORDER
the provisional execution of the judgment of this motion notwithstanding
an appeal;”

[
3
]

The Curator seeks somewhat similar conclusions
but goes further by requesting,
inter alia
, that the Power of attorney
and Mandate in case of incapacity signed by De. on October 3
rd
, 2011
in favour of her sister Madam R. P. (“
R.
”) be revoked and declared null
and void. The conclusions of the Curator’s Motion read as follows:

“
REVOKE
AND DECLARE
null and void the document entitled
"POWER OF ATTORNEY AND MANDATE IN CASE OF INCAPACITY" signed on
October 3, 2011, before the notary, Gergana Hristova, under number four hundred
twenty-two (422) of said notary's minutes;

DECLARE
null and void all mandates, wills, and other legal documents which
the respondent of full age, De. P. may have signed, and this, as of November 1,
2010
;

ORDER,
on order of meeting signed by a judge or clerk of the Superior Court
of the district of Montreal, the calling of a meeting of relatives, persons
connected by marriage or a civil union and friends, to deliberate and issue its
opinion on the object of this motion;

ORDER
the meeting of family and friends to deliberate and issue an opinion
on the appropriateness of:

I-
instituting protective supervision in the interests of the respondent of full
age, De. P.;

II-
determining that the appropriate form of protective supervision for the respondent
of full age, De. P., is that of curatorship to the person and property;

Ill-
appointing the Curateur public du Québec, curator to the person and property of
the respondent of full age, De. P.;

IV- and
to deliberate and issue its opinion on any other question that the Court or the
Clerk deems appropriate to submit to its attention.

IF THE MEETING OF RELATIVES,
PERSONS CONNECTED BY MARRIAGE OR A CIVIL UNION AND FRIENDS CANNOT BE HELD
BECAUSE OF AN INADEQUATE NUMBER OF MEMBERS OR THEIR COMPLETE ABSENCE ALTHOUGH
DULY ORDERED TO MEET,
to declare the institution of
protective supervision on behalf of

the respondent of full age, De. P.,
without said meeting being held;

DECLARE
the institution of protective supervision in the interests of the
respondent of full age, De. P.;

DETERMINE
that the appropriate form of protective supervision for the
respondent of full age, De. P., is that of curatorship to the person and
property;

APPOINT
the Curateur public du Québec, curator to the person and property of
the respondent of full age, De. P.;

ENTRUST
guardianship of the respondent of full age, De. P., to the Curateur
public du Québec;

TO ORDER
the provisional execution of the judgment on this motion, any appeal
notwithstanding;”

[
4
]

Although the present proceedings to declare the
institution of a protective supervision for De. were initiated in November
2011, such an order has yet to be made as the present proceedings have been the
theatre of bitter and acrimonious debates from the outset. Even the
circumstances leading to their institution are somewhat peculiar, if not
troubling and disturbing.

[
5
]

J. and De. were married on March 17, 2007. They
never had children. At the time of the wedding, J., previously divorced twice,
was 44 years old while De. was a 58 year-old single woman. The couple had known
each other for a significant period of time as they met in 1991. Before her
wedding, De. had been residing at her mother’s house for most of her life.

[
6
]

Unfortunately, over the recent years, De.
developed a serious illness that has been incapacitating her progressively to
the point where she could no longer stay at home unsupervised while her husband
was going to work. J. arranged to have help at home while he was at work. When
the help was not available, a system was arranged whereby he would drive De. in
the morning to her mother’s house where her sister R. also lives as the latter
looks after their aging mother. J. would pick up De. in the late afternoon upon
his return from work and the couple would return home where J. would continue
looking after the needs of his wife.

[
7
]

On November 9, 2011, this routine was altered
abruptly and unexpectedly as R. suddenly denied to J. access to his wife De..
This situation persists to this day and J. has since not only been prevented
from seeing his own wife but De.’s family prevents all forms of communications
between De. and J., pretexting that it results exclusively from De.’s will.

[
8
]

On the following day, November 10, 2011, J.
sought the help of the police to retrieve his wife, who informed him after
investigation that even if he was De.’s husband, there was nothing that they
could do for him as R., keeping De. at their mother’s residence, was holding a
Power of attorney and that divorce proceedings had apparently been instituted
against him; R. also claiming to hold a restraining order against him.

[
9
]

At that time, J. was totally unaware that his
wife wanted to divorce him and wanted to seek a restraining order against him
as she apparently feared for her life in his presence. J. did not know either
that on October 3
rd
, 2011, his wife had executed before notary, M
tre

Gergana Hristova (“
Hristova
”), a Power of Attorney and a Mandate in case
of incapacity pursuant to which De. appointed R. as her attorney and her
mandatary in case of incapacity (
IP-7
) (collectively referred to as the
“
Mandate
” or the “
Power of Attorney
”).

[
10
]

The Mandate also stipulated that De.’s other
sister, Mrs. C. P. (“
C.
”) and C.’s daughter, De.’s niece, Mrs. T. B. (“
T.
”)
were substitute mandataries should R. be incapable of acting as attorney or
mandatary for De..

[
11
]

On November 9, 2011, when J. dropped his wife at
R.’s house as usual, he was totally unaware that while he was at work on
October 3
rd
, his sisters-in-law, R. and C., had secretly arranged
for his wife to attend the offices of notary Hristova to sign the Power of
Attorney and the Mandate a few weeks earlier. It had never been discussed
between them. J. was totally unaware neither that this was the last time that
he would ever see his wife and that she was going to serve upon him divorce
proceedings two days later. He was totally unaware that on that day, November
9, 2011, the activity that R. had planned for her sister was a visit at a
lawyer’s office to have divorce proceeding together with an
“urgent”
motion for interim measures seeking a restraining order against
him, a man depicted as erratic, unpredictable and violent to such an extent
that De. and R. were fearing for their lives. Moreover, J. was trying to poison
his wife by forcing her to take drugs without her consent.

[
12
]

J. claimed that his relationship with his wife
was good despite her growing declining health, which was an important source of
concern for him but that he was nevertheless committed to offering his wife the
best possible care. His dedication to his wife and excellent care are reflected
in several doctors’ notes in De.’s medical files.

[
13
]

Two days later, on November 11, 2011, J.’s prior
warning from the previous day became reality. He was served with divorce
proceedings initiated by De. on November 10, 2011. These proceedings came as a
total shock to him and lead J. to believe very strongly that the signing of the
Mandate and the divorce proceedings were masterminded by De.’s sisters, R. and C.
(referred to collectively as the “
Sisters
”), who had been in constant
conflict with him about De.’s true state of health since it started failing in
early 2010. At that time, the Sisters had been systematically at odds with him
for more than a year as they strongly disagreed with De.’s medical diagnosis as
well as with the medical help that J. was seeking for his wife. Their
disagreement regarding De.’s medical treatments stemmed from the fact that the
Sisters did not believe for a single moment that their sister De. was actually
suffering from
“Frontotemporal dementia”,
a frontotemporal lobar degeneration of the brain (“
FTD
”)
since early 2010 and formally diagnosed in November 2010.

[
14
]

As in their personal opinion De. was not
suffering from FTD, the Sisters were challenging each and every treatment
sought by J. for De. despite the fact that he was following the recommendations
of physicians who confirmed her unfortunate diagnosis. At all relevant times,
the Sisters maintained that De. was not suffering from dementia but from a
temporary speech impediment that only required speech therapy provided by R. to
her sister.

[
15
]

Given their strong opposition, the Sisters
believed that J.’s help was, on the contrary, highly detrimental to De.’s
health and placed her in grave danger. Even giving her B12 vitamins was life
threatening, in their personal views.

[
16
]

In other words, by November 2011, the Sisters
had to get De. out of the sphere of bad influence that J. was exerting on his
wife; a man, in any event, that she should have never married, as the evidence
will reveal.

-

The procedural context

[
17
]

As previously mentioned, some thirty-six hours
after J. was first denied access to his wife by R. on a permanent basis, J. was
served with the divorce proceedings that contained a motion for interim
emergency measures. Among those measures, De. requested that her husband be
ordered not to communicate, directly or indirectly with herself or with any
other member of her family, given J.’s conduct and danger to De.’s mental and
physical wellbeing. According to a detailed affidavit executed by De. (
IB-2
),
she expressed her
“fear for her life”
and
the need that J. be restrained from coming within 200 yards from her (new)
residence where she was now living with R. and their mother.

[
18
]

The divorce proceedings, filed by her attorney
Liebman & Associés, appear to have been signed by De. on November 10, 2011.
Within a few days, M
tre
Irwin I. Liebman (“
Liebman
”) was
substituted by M
tre
Lillian Kliger (“
Kliger
”) who also
represented her in the present proceedings. Although the divorce proceedings
have been contested by J., no restraining order was ever issued by the Superior
Court regarding the interim emergency provisional measures sought by De.…and R..

[
19
]

On November 24, 2011, J. initiated the present
proceedings to institute a protective supervision for De., the J. Motion.

[
20
]

The Sisters view the present proceedings as a
form of illegal defence to De.’s legitimate divorce proceedings.

[
21
]

However, J. firmly believes that at all relevant
times, his wife never contemplated divorcing him and that in any event, in
November 2011, she was incapable of making such an important decision, let
alone understand the legal ramifications of the Mandate and of the divorce
proceedings. In other words, she could not have given a free and enlightened
consent when she signed the Mandate on October 3
rd
and the divorce
proceedings on November 10, 2011; both at the behest and in the presence of R.
and/or C..

[
22
]

As previously indicate, Kliger filed an
appearance on behalf of her client De. in the J. Motion and substituted Liebman
in the divorce proceedings.

[
23
]

On December 8 and 9, 2011, De. and J. appeared
before Mister Justice Tingley (“
Tingley J.
”) with their respective
attorneys on a Motion for a safeguard order filed by J. who was trying to
regain access to his wife. R. was also present and represented herself.

[
24
]

The main issue at that hearing was to determine
if pending the proceedings, De. should return to the care of her husband after
a month and a half of absence. After a day and a half of hearing, Tingley J.
indicated that he preferred to err on the side of caution and decided that for
the time being De. should remain under the care of R. as the latter had been
taking care of De. since November 9, 2011.

[
25
]

Although there is no written judgment, the full
transcripts of the two-day hearing reveal that Tingley J. favoured the
status
quo
clearly expecting however that the parties would proceed diligently on
the merits. His sense of urgency was obvious; the
status quo
could not
be maintained for long.

[
26
]

Unfortunately, it is exactly the opposite that
occurred.

[
27
]

Ten months later, on October 16 and 17, 2012,
the J. Motion was to proceed on the merits but on the second day, Madam Justice
Gaudreau (“
Gaudreau J.
”) determined that the hearing could no longer
continue without a psychosocial assessment that she felt was absolutely
necessary in order to rule on the merits of the J. motion. Gaudreau J. rendered
an order in accordance and that a psychosocial assessment be prepared. At that
hearing, De. was always represented by Kliger and this time, R. was represented
by her cousin, M
tre
John Wiseman (“
Wiseman
”), although he did
not file an appearance on her behalf.

[
28
]

On December 14, 2012, Kliger filed on behalf of De.
a Motion to dismiss the J. Motion based on Article 54.1 of the
Code of civil
procedure
claiming that it was abusive. The affidavit in support of De.’s
Motion to dismiss was not signed by De. but rather by R.:

“2. That by virtue of a Power of
Attorney, identified as Exhibit D-2 in the present file, I have been
constituted mandatary for my sister, the Respondent, with powers to represent
her in any actions concerning her and her property;”

[
29
]

On December 20, 2012, Mister Justice Jean-Yves
Lalonde (“
Lalonde J.
”) ordered that the psychosocial assessment
previously ordered by Gaudreau J. be filed on January 31, 2013 at the latest by
Mrs. Nicole Souaid (“
Souaid
”), the social worker who had been mandated
to prepare it. Lalonde J. also set the hearing on the De.’s Motion to dismiss
to March 26, 2013.

[
30
]

Madam Justice Le Bel (“
Le Bel J.
”) heard
the parties on De.’s Motion to dismiss on March 26 and 27, 2013. Just as it was
at the hearing before Gaudreau J., De. was not present in the courtroom, nor
was she called upon to testify. In fact, the court records show that De.
actually only appeared briefly before Tingley J. in December 2011. At the March
2013 hearing, R. was present and was once again representing herself as Wiseman
never filed an appearance on her behalf.

[
31
]

On March 27, 2013, Le Bel J. dismissed De.’s
Motion to dismiss and issued the following orders
[1]
:

« [46]
REJETTE
la requête pour rejet amendée;

[47]
ORDONNE
que la soussignée demeure saisie du dossier au moins pour assurer
sa mise en état;

[48]
ORDONNE
la suspension des procédures dans le dossier de divorce en
attendant un jugement dans le présent dossier, usant des pouvoirs que lui
confère l’
article 274

C.c.Q
.;

[49]

DÉSIGNE
provisoirement le Curateur public du Québec pour administrer les
biens de madame et lui
ORDONNE
de faire le nécessaire pour mettre le
dossier en état et obtenir un jugement du Tribunal sur la requête en ouverture
d’un régime de protection
;

[50]
En particulier, le Curateur
public devra vérifier le contenu du dossier, la preuve déjà faite et la mettre
dans une forme qui pourra être soumise au Tribunal, ajouter au dossier toute
preuve jugée nécessaire pour compléter le dossier
, et
DÉCLARE

que le rapport d’un ergothérapeute serait important pour apprécier la capacité
de madame, ses besoins, l’encadrement et les soins dont elle a besoin
.
Le
Curateur public pourra ajouter toute autre preuve, médicale ou autre, jugée
nécessaire par le Curateur public
;

[51]
DÉCLARE
madame forclose de produire un rapport d’expert médical puisqu’elle
ne l’a pas fait dans le délai fixé par l’honorable juge Gaudreau, sauf
permission du Tribunal sur une requête à cet effet;

[52]
SUGGÈRE
fortement qu’on obtienne et produise au dossier le rapport d’un
ergothérapeute
;

[53]
ORDONNE
que madame continue de résider dans sa famille;

[54]
ORDONNE
la communication au Curateur public ou à une personne mandatée par
lui, de tout le dossier concernant madame P., ce qui inclut son dossier médical
ou tout autre dossier qui pourrait être protégé par le secret professionnel, ce
qui n’inclut pas un dossier d’avocat;

[55]
ORDONNE
au greffier de transmettre la présente ordonnance au Curateur
public sous pli recommandé;

[56] Le Tribunal reste saisi du
dossier.  Les parties ou le Curateur public pourront communiquer avec le
Tribunal pour des directives ou pour fixer une date d’audition. »

[Emphasis added]

[The “
Le Bel Judgment
”]

[
32
]

Incidentally, pursuant to the Le Bel Judgment,
the judge ordered,
inter alia
, the stay of the pending divorce
proceedings until judgment is rendered on the J. Motion.

[
33
]

On June 13, 2013, the Court of appeal dismissed De.’s
appeal of the Le Bel Judgment
[2]
. Of particular interest are the following comments of Madam Justice
Bich (“
Bich J.
”):

[34]
Instead of challenging
LeBel J.'s judgment, the appellant and her lawyer (as well as her family)
should ensure that the action before the Superior Court proceeds as quickly and
efficiently as possible
,
this being an important and urgent matter that
must be resolved with utmost diligence from all parties
.
Special
attention shall be required from the Public Curator, who is provisionally in
charge of the appellant's property and who is also in charge of
“
faire le nécessaire pour mettre le dossier
en état et obtenir un jugement du Tribunal sur la requête en ouverture d'un
régime de protection
”.
[3]

[35] It is to be noted that the
inscription in appeal as well as the motion to dismiss the appeal were served
on the Public Curator, who chose not to appear in the file.
This will not
preclude the Court from ordering him to act as diligently as possible in the
present file
.

[Emphasis added]

[
34
]

A few days later, the Curator filed an
appearance in the present case with his own Motion to,
inter alia
,
revoke and to declare null and void the Mandate as well as any other will,
mandate and other legal documents that De. may have executed since she was
diagnosed with FTD in November 2010. The Curator added C. and T. as impleaded
parties given the fact that they were designated as substitute mandataries to R.
pursuant to the Mandate. Like J., the Curator also sought the institution of a
protective supervision with respect to De..

[
35
]

On December 30, 2013, M
tre
Mao
Chambers (“
Chambers
”), who works with Kliger in the same premises, filed
an appearance on behalf of C. and T..

[
36
]

On January 23, 2014, the parties appeared again
before Le Bel J. for a management conference.

[
37
]

Chambers, acting on behalf of C. and T., was
seeking the immediate dismissal of the Curator’s Motion. According to the
minutes of the hearing, Kliger stated that henceforth she was not only
representing the interest of De., the mandatary of the Mandate, but those of R.,
the mandatory as well. Kliger echoed the position of Chambers on the
inadmissibility of the Curator’s Motion who had no legal interest to interject
into a private matter.

[
38
]

M
tre
Paulene Massillon (“
Massillon
”),
who represents the Curator, challenged on an ethical basis the right of Kigler
to represent De. and R. at the same time. According to Massillon, Kliger placed
herself in a clear conflict of interest situation and the same applied to
Chambers, who works in the same office. De. should have an independent counsel
under the present circumstances.

[
39
]

Upon reading the minutes of the said hearing,
both Kliger and Chambers had the same position regarding De.; the latter was at
all relevant and still at that time competent and certainly not inapt. Based on
their unified position, the J. Motion and the Curator Motion seeking to
institute a regime of protective supervision concerning De., both had to be
dismissed as De. was not inapt then and back in October 2011 as well as when she
executed the Mandate. It should not be revoked.

[
40
]

The minutes of that management conference
confirm that Kliger and Chambers were contesting De.’s inaptitude
[4]
. However, Kliger announced that in the event that the incapacity of
De. is eventually established, she would then seek to have the Mandate homologated
by the Court. But, given the fact that in their view, De. was indeed apt, there
was no need for her Mandate to be homologated at that time.

[
41
]

If she was apt, how is it that De. could not
even sign her own affidavit in support of her proceedings seeking the dismissal
of the J. Motion?

[
42
]

At the January 23, 2013 conference, Chambers was
also given a certain delay by Le Bel J. to produce a counter-expertise
establishing that De. was capable when she executed the Mandate. While it
appeared somewhat odd that such a request would come from the lawyer
representing the substitute mandataries and not from De.’s own lawyer, who now
happened to also represent the principal beneficiary of the Mandate, it was
easily explained by the fact that pursuant to the Le Bel Judgment, De. and
Kliger were estopped from doing so for failing to file a medical expertise on
her capacity within the delay previously granted by Gaudreau J.

[
43
]

The evidence will reveal that Chambers will file
an expert’s report prepared by the psychiatrist Christophe Nowakowski that was,
to all intents and purposes, a carbon copy of the report that he had prepared
for Kliger as the latter had failed to file the same as ordered by Gaudreau J.
within five weeks from October 17, 2012.

[
44
]

On March 25, 2014, the Curator filed a Motion
seeking the disqualification of Kliger and Chambers due to the fact that the
current issues raised or faced by their clients placed them in positions of
conflict of interest.

[
45
]

The Curator alleged in his Motion to disqualify
Kliger and Chambers that based on the medical assessment of De. made by Dr.
Catherine Ferrier (“
Ferrier
”) on September 10 and October 15, 2013 and
confirmed in a letter dated November 12, 2013 (
IP-5
), De. was then totally
and permanently inapt to look after her own person and her affairs due to the
diagnosis of FTD made earlier by two neurologists.

[
46
]

With this information on hand, the Curator
believed that when Kliger decided to act on behalf of R. and her colleague Chambers
on behalf of C. and T., De. was not capable of consenting and giving proper
instructions to her lawyer Kliger who, as a result thereof, placed herself in a
position to share with R. confidential information obtained from De..

[
47
]

Moreover, notwithstanding the medical findings
concerning De.’s total and permanent inaptitude, R., her mandatary, was
contesting actively, if not vigorously, the same findings arguing that her
sister was not incapable. C. and T., the substitute mandataries, adopted the
same position. They all claimed to act in accordance with the true wishes of De.
who, since December 2011, never came to Court once to voice her wishes to a
judge.

[
48
]

De. was not present during the hearing on the
Curator’s Motion to disqualify her own attorney in order to confirm her wishes
and express her consent that her lawyer Kliger could act as well for her sister
R. and may disclose to her sister or share with her personal information
protected by professional secrecy.

[
49
]

The Curator expressed the opinion that De. did
not have the capacity to waive the professional secrecy to which she is
entitled by law.

[
50
]

C. and T., who both live in the USA, must have
felt that they had sufficient interests in these matters to warrant the
appointment of a lawyer and they chose the one who worked with Kliger in the
same office.

[
51
]

The Curator expressed his concerns that
confidential and privileged information concerning De. may be leaked to Chamber
who incidentally, took a very active role in the present proceedings.

[
52
]

As previously indicated, De. did not attend at
Court to signify her understanding and agreement that another lawyer working
with Kliger in the same office space could represent her sister C. and her
niece T. with the risk that private and confidential information of hers be
leaked to C. and T. through their new lawyer.

[
53
]

In any event, the undersigned heard the
Curator’s Motion in disqualification in September 2014, based on the evidence
and more particularly, based on the testimonies of R., C. and T., leaving no
doubt about their respective opinions that De. was not inapt then or before and
validly consented to her lawyer Kliger representing R. at the same time and
consented as well to C. and T. being represented by the lawyer Chambers. The
Court decided, given De.’s absence and her family’s strong contestation
regarding her alleged incapacity, that it was in the interest of justice and of
all parties to postpone the decision on the Motion to disqualify Kliger and
Chambers until the Court has had the opportunity to determine whether De. was
indeed capable of understanding the implications of her lawyer representing at
the same time her sister R. and of giving a valid informed consent thereto; the
same concept applying to her other sister C. and her niece T. being represented
by Kliger’s colleague.

[
54
]

Under such circumstances, the Curator’s Motion
to disqualify was therefore suspended until the Court could dispose of the
present two Motions and ultimately determine among other things, if De. was
capable in October 2011 to validly execute the Mandate and if the latter was at
the time indeed capable of executing the same, if De. became inapt afterwards,
warranting the institution of a protection supervision of De. to ensure the
protection of her person, the administration of her patrimony and generally,
the exercise of her civil rights.

[
55
]

Hopefully, the evidence adduced at that hearing
could also serve to determine as well whether De. was capable of understanding
and giving a valid consent to R. being represented by her own lawyer and C. and
T. being represented by her lawyer’s colleague in December 2013.

[
56
]

In other words, given the contradictory evidence
adduced at the hearing on the Motion to disqualify, evidence that hinged
heavily on De.’s alleged capacity, it was deemed that there should be no
further delays in hearing the J. Motion and the Curator Motion on the merits in
order to determine, once and for all, whether De.’s alleged incapacity existed
or not and in the affirmative, since when.

THE HEARING ON
THE PRESENT MOTIONS

[
57
]

At the outset, the Court ruled that the parties
would proceed with the Curator Motion and that the evidence would be common as
well to the J. Motion to the extent applicable. A single judgment would be
rendered on both Motions with the Court’s understanding that it would restrict
its findings, at this stage of the proceedings, on the following issues only:

-

evaluation as to De.’s mental capacity, both generally and more specifically
pertaining to her capacity to decide to whom she wished to give a power of
attorney and also her mental capacity to decide that she wanted to divorce (
D-13
).

[
352
]

The Court understands that Nowakowski’s opinion,
on October 14, 2012, can be summarized as follows:
“it is not
obvious that “De.” suffers from mental incapacity in regards to the two issues
previously mentioned [Power of Attorney and divorce], and that her mental
capacity can be obscured to the casual observer by her speech impairment
(
D-13
).”

[
353
]

His initial report dated July 29, 2013 (
R-22
) and requested
by Kliger, concluded that De. “
certainly
”
had the mental capacity to take the decision to divorce and to decide whom she
would like to take care of her affairs and to express her decision by signing
the Mandate. The psychiatrist concluded his report with:
“Due to the
communication deficit, other cognitive functions are very difficult to assess.”

[
354
]

As previously mentioned earlier in this
judgment, the 2013 report was not filed as De. was estopped from filing the
same by the Le Bel Judgment and it was replaced via Chambers, the lawyer for C.
and T. with an almost identical second report dated February 28, 2014, in which
Nowakowski reached essentially the same conclusions regarding De.’s capacity to
execute the Mandate:

“In the latter half of 2012, Ms. P.
had the mental capacity to decide whom she would like to take care of her
affairs and to express her decision, and her illness being a progressive one,
she certainly had that capacity at the time that she signed a mandate in
anticipation of incapacity, in October 2011.

Ms. P. currently needs assistance
with managing her health, her assets and her daily needs. This is most clearly
due to her incapacity to communicate clearly with most people. Abulia, Apraxia
and motor slowing also contribute to this incapacity. Due to the communication deficit,
other cognitive functions are very difficult to assess.”

[
355
]

The Court understands that the psychiatrist met
with De. on September 25 and December 4, 2012 and observed her at the Montreal
courthouse on October 17, 2012 and January 17, 2013. The court record shows
that De. did not appear before Gaudreau J. on October 17, 2012 and there is no
indication of any court appearances on January 17, 2013.

[
356
]

Nowakowski disagreed with Chertkow and Ferrier,
who both stated that it was not possible for them to do a retrospective
evaluation of De.’s mental capacity in October 2011.

[
357
]

Although her language impairment was such that
it is impossible to carry out tests adding “
we are completely clueless at what she
wants
”, the psychiatrist nevertheless testified
that it was not impossible and that the most likely conclusion might be that
since he found that De. had a marginal capacity to make a mandate in case of
incapacity in December 2012, she necessarily had to be in better position
fourteen months earlier in October 2011. In other words, the Court understands
that if De. was marginally apt in December 2012, she had to be apt in October
2011 as her condition might have been less severe back then.

[
358
]

Nowakowski added that while De. could not decide
to sell shares, she could decide on who should be looking after her.

[
359
]

His assessment was that there were odds of 75 %
to 80 % in favour that De. was apt in October 2011, with however a “
large error
margin

[une grosse marge
d’erreur]
”.

[
360
]

At his first meeting with De. at his office in
September 2012, De. was speaking very little and could not make complete
sentences. Three months later in December 2012, when the psychiatrist
determined that De. had
“marginal capacity”,
he
noted that she could only respond by circling suggested answers on a piece
paper. He did not see her write.

[
361
]

Nowakowski did not perform any tests with De. to
assess her level of comprehension on account of her communication difficulties
that could possibly vitiate any results. He anticipated very low scores due to
her language difficulties. Under such circumstances, he could not determine
whether the low scores would be due to her lack of comprehension or to her
speech impediments.

[
362
]

“I cannot really say that I had an interview in the usual sense of the
term with De. due to her inability to speak.”
Nowakowski
added that he basically spent time with De. and tried to speak with her during
his sessions with her.

[
363
]

The February 2014 report that was very similar,
if not somewhat identical to the July 2013 report, basically excluded his
conclusion regarding the divorce proceedings. His findings were still based on
his December 2012 meeting with De.. The psychiatrist did not meet again with De.
after the meetings that served to prepare his 2013 report in order to prepare
his second report in 2014.

[
364
]

Basically, the Court retains from the
psychiatrist’s testimony that on one hand, De.’s communication deficits were so
severe that any test could not realistically yield reliable results with
respect to her level of comprehension and her mental capacity, leaving
nevertheless odds between 75 %-80 % with a large error margin that
she was mentally competent when she executed the Mandate in October 2013. His
2013 report also had the same conclusion for the divorce proceedings.

[
365
]

On the other hand, the Court considered as well:

-

Dr. Sidani, a neurologist, who gave the opinion
on November 21, 2011 to the effect that De. was already partially permanently
inapt (
R-5
);

-

Dr. Ferrier, a specialist in geriatric medicine,
who declared De. totally inapt as a result of her meeting with her in September
2013 and who testified that she could not do a retrospection assessment of De.’s
mental capacity in October and November 2011 (
IP-5
); and

-

Dr. Chertkow, a cognitive neurologist, who
wrote,
inter alia
:

▪

On May 10, 2012 (
IP-4
)
:
“The patient as last time, was very
passive and abulic and rather perplexed during the interview. She had some
deshinibation. Speech was very impaired. Her last MoCA was 9/30.”

▪

On November 1, 2012 (
IP-10
):

“I understand that she is being seen for
competency assessment by Dr. Nowakowski. I find her to be very cognitively
impaired with a MoCA test of 8/30. I find her competency to be very
questionable but again it is hard to know because she is simply not cooperative
for a lot of the cognitive testing”;

[
366
]

Dr. Nowakowski stated that he disagreed with Dr.
Chertkow and that Dr. Sidani’s opinion given on November 21, 2011, a few days
only after the institution of the divorce proceedings and a little more than a
month after the execution of the Mandate, did not change his opinion.

[
367
]

With all due respect, after considering the
evidence as a whole, the Court cannot retain the opinion of Dr. Nowakowski.

[
368
]

As previously indicated and notwithstanding the
professional opinions to the contrary, the preponderant evidence still leads
the Court to entertain serious doubts, very serious doubts that as of August 1
st
,
2011, De. was mentally competent, let alone capable to decide on her own and to
execute the Power of Attorney and the Mandate on October 3, 2011. The same very
serious doubts apply to her capacity to making a free and enlightened decision
on the institution of divorce proceedings on November 10, 2011.

[
369
]

The Court cannot ignore either the cognitive
tests (MoCA) made since 2010.

[
370
]

In November 2010, the MoCA test yielded a 20/30
result. In April 2011, it was down to 15/30, in February 2012, 9/30 and in
May 2012, 8/30.

[
371
]

Without being the basis of the Court’s present
ruling, those results nevertheless reinforce the serious doubts of De.’s
alleged capacity as of August 1
st
, 2011 and thereafter.

[
372
]

In the previously cited case of
G.D. vs Ge.D.
,
Guibault J. wrote as follows on the MMSE (Mini-Mental State Exam) being the
predecessor to the Montreal Cognitive Assessment
[16]

(MoCA) test:

« [91]
Tant la
jurisprudence que la doctrine établissent qu'un résultat de 20/30 au test MMSE
est un minimum pour conclure à la capacité d'une personne à signer un mandat
d'inaptitude ou un testament.
Dans la cause de
M.B.
c.
D.B.
[17]
, un
jugement prononcé par la juge Hélène Poulin en avril 2005, le résultat au MMSE
était de 24/30, alors que dans le dossier
P.M.
et
A.O.
[18]
, un
jugement de l'honorable Jean-Pierre Chrétien du 9 octobre 2008, le
résultat au même test était de 23/30, et dans les deux cas le Tribunal a refusé
l'homologation d'un mandat d'inaptitude.

[92] Il faut se rappeler que dans
le présent dossier, le résultat obtenu par madame G... n'était que de 17/30,
plus d'un an avant la signature du mandat, et il a été établi qu'il y a eu
détérioration entre 2008 et 2009. La preuve présentée par les requérants
établissant l'incapacité de madame G... de consentir valablement à un mandat
d'inaptitude en novembre 2009 est fort concluante et, suivant la jurisprudence,
il appartenait à Ge... d'établir la capacité de sa mère lorsqu'il a décidé de
la conduire chez le notaire Filiatrault pour qu'elle signe les deux
documents : un mandat au cas d'inaptitude et un testament. »

[Emphasis added]

[
373
]

In conclusion, the Court finds that the evidence
is sufficient compelling, if not overwhelming and the doubts about De.’s
incapacity are so serious to warrant a determination that as of August 1
st
,
2011, De. was incapable to take care of herself and to administer her property
and has remained incapable until now.

[
374
]

In light of the foregoing findings, the Court
will also revoke and will declare null and void
ab initio
the Power of
Attorney and the Mandate in case of incapacity executed before notary G.
Hristova in the same deed by De. on October 3
rd
, 2011 (
IP-7
).

[
375
]

As well, in November 2011, De., who was still
being highly vulnerable and highly susceptible to the influences exerted upon
her by her Sisters, did not have the legal capacity to institute divorce
proceedings against her husband let alone the capacity make such an important
decision.

[
376
]

Given the fact that as of August 1
st
,
2011, in the Court’s opinion, De. was undoubtedly inapt, has remained inapt
until now, given that De. was also inapt when

she executed the divorce proceedings, given the provisions of

Article 2167.1
[19]
of the
Civil code of Quebec
, given the compelling evidence
and the Court’s findings on the circumstances surrounding the institution of
the divorce proceedings (file number 500-12-311270-114), the Court will declare
that De. was legally incompetent and was incapable as well to give a free and
enlightened consent to the said divorce proceedings on November 10
th
,
2011.

[
377
]

The divorce proceedings instituted under court
number 500-12-311270-114 by De., an inapt person at the time, should have never
been instituted by a person incapable to make such a major decision and will
therefore be declared null and void
ab initio
.

[
378
]

With the benefit of the extensive and compelling
evidence adduced before this Court, it is quite opportune to reiterate and
recall the perspicacious comments of Tingley J. made in December 2011, a few
days only after the institution of the divorce proceedings, bearing in mind
that he was the only judge who had the benefit of seeing and hearing De.:

“What I find… Quite frankly, what I
find extraordinary is that divorce proceedings would have been taken while De.
is still back-and-forth, coming home at night, back home and then going… It
smacks, quite frankly, maître, it smacks a little bit of controls, and I don’t
know which side is the controller and who’s the controlee, but maybe the family
is stepping in here and stirring a pot that really doesn’t need stirring.

[…]

I guess I'm distressed to see that
proceedings in divorce have been taken in a situation where I don't think De.
knows what's being asked of her.

[…]

I think there's ... I think there
probably is a degree of manipulation here, but I could be wrong, and I'm not
the one who's going to make that determination today.

[…]

But I don't think she was even
competent to sign that document, from what I've seen today. So you know, that
kind of a proceeding is... is going to be subject to ...
I
don't know what
it's going to be subject to, but it's ... it seems to me that we are
complicating something unnecessarily.

[…]

And there's been... there's been an
alienation here and... Or let me put it this way: there appears that there may
have been alienation, and I'm speaking now of the husband. So these are things
that I've seen in the last day and a half that I guess make me a little bit
uneasy about how this file is going to unfold. But I do think that the sooner
you get to a family council... And don't forget the family council is going to
be loaded with members of De.'s family; I don't know who is going to be from
husband's side, but ...

[…]

Yeah. But I am very uneasy about a
lawyer accepting her signature in her condition, O.K., on divorce proceedings.
I am very uneasy. I have to tell you that right now: very uneasy…”

the Curator to declare null and void all mandates, wills, and other legal

st
, 2011, De. was incapable

De. executed between November 1
st
, 2010 and August 1
st
,
2011 any other legal documents including a will that could raise suspicion as

[
382
]

make herein such a declaration of nullity in addition to the others already

st
,
2010 under the present circumstances.

]

[20]
.

and the Curator in their respective Motions to declare the institution of

ab

It is very unfortunate that it took three and a
half years to confirm the preliminary findings of the first judge to be
involved in this senseless saga. Three and a half years during which De. was
deprived of her right to be with her husband and during which her husband was
also deprived of remaining with his wife who has sadly continued to sink into
her illness. Three and a half years during which J. was prevented from
continuing caring for her despite the fact that he was already doing a
“fantastic job”.

[
393
]

At this point, the Court cannot keep silent on
two disturbing issues that came to light during J.’s cross-examination by
Kliger, the lawyer for De., the mandatory and R., the mandatary, at the same
time. From the Court’s stand point, a fruitless attempt was made to depict J.
as an uncaring husband, who was quoted by the lawyer as saying on one hand
”My wife needs
all of her loved ones around her”
and yet, on
the other hand, J. would keep on bringing De. to her mother’s house (R.’s
house). The Court understood that if J. really loved De., he should have looked
after her at home instead of dropping De. at R.’s home on week days. Having to
be temporarily absent from one’s home to earn the financial support for the
household does not tantamount to lack of love or lack of caring for a spouse
who is ill and who requires care. That is precisely the role of other family
members to extend help when one member cannot especially considering that J.’s
absences were to generate an income for the couple. J.’s absences were not only
justified, but they were also warranted to be able to offer the best care and
support for his wife. J. should never be blamed for that.

[
394
]

The lawyer, presumably trying to establish once
again that J. was not a caring and loving husband, asked him to explain why if
he really loved De., he never sent any money to his wife over all these years. J.
answered:

“You kidnap a person and now you
want a ransom?”

[
395
]

Kliger concluded her cross-examination with that
answer.

[
396
]

Maybe that the witness could have answered as
well that he was forced instead to spend a lot of money on these senseless
legal proceedings.

[
397
]

Based on the evidence, the Court believes that
if De. had not been taken away from her husband, J. would have continued to
exhibit the love and commitment to care for his wife on all fronts, including
financial. The evaluations made at J.’s home with De., which were filed in the
court record, evidence that finding.

[
398
]

In any event, J. certainly does not have to bear
or to assume any of the financial responsibilities and consequences of abusive
and malicious decisions made and of malevolent deeds committed by some members
of the
“P. Family”
in violation of De.’s and J.’s
rights as a married couple.
